{{RunningHeader|Thargelion|6266|that}}'''Thargelion''' (thär-gē′li-on), ''n.'' [< Gr. Θαργηλιών, < Θαργήλια, the festival Thargelia: see ''Thargelia.''] The eleventh month of the ancient Attic calendar, containing thirty days, and corresponding to the last part of May and the first part of June. '''tharldome†''', ''n.'' Same as ''thraldom.'' '''tharm''' (thärm), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''therm'', Sc. ''thairm''; < ME. ''tharm'', ''therm'', < AS. ''thearm'' = OFries. ''therm'', ''thirm'' = D. MLG. ''darm'' = OHG. ''daram'', MHG. G. ''darm'' = Icel. ''tharmr'' = Sw. Dan. ''tarm'', gut, = L. ''trames'', way, = Gr. τράμις, tharm, gut; cf. τρῆμα, hole, ear, < τετραίνειν (√ τρα), bore through.] An intestine; an entrail; gut. [Obsolete or dialectal.] {{smaller block|Eustathius . . . doth tell that in old time they made their bow-strings of bullocks' ''thermes'', which they twined together as they}} {{smaller block|''That'' it went hand in hand even with the vow. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 5. 49.}}}} {{smaller block|Majesty never was vested to ''that'' degree in the Person of the King ''as'' not to be more conspicuous and more august in Parliament, as I have often shown. {{right|''Milton'', Ans. to Salmasius.}}}} 2. Used absolutely or without a noun as a demonstrative pronoun. {{smaller|(''a'') To indicate a person or thing already referred to or implied, or specially pointed at or otherwise indicated, and having generally the same force and significance as when used as an adjective: as, give me ''that''; do you see ''that''?}} {{smaller block|Foretell new storms to ''those'' already spent. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1589.}}}} {{smaller block|What springal is ''that''? ha! ''Shirley'', Love Tricks, ii. 1.}} {{smaller block|From hence forward be ''that'' which thine own brutish silence hath made thee. {{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, Pref., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|She has ''that'' in her aspect against which it is impossible}} book ''from which'' I read, the spot ''near which'' he stood, the pay ''for which'' he works; but not the man ''of that'' I spoke, etc., though one may say, the man ''that'' I spoke ''of'', the book ''that'' I read ''from'', the place ''that'' he stood ''near'', the pay ''that'' he works ''for'', and so on. When the relative clause conveys an additional idea or statement, or is parenthetical, ''who'' and ''which'' are in modern English rather to be used than ''that:'' thus, "James, ''whom'' I saw yesterday, told me," but not "James ''that'', etc." ''That'' more often introduces a restrictive or definitive clause, but ''who'' and ''which'' are frequently used in the same way. See ''who.'' {{smaller block|Lord God, ''that'' lens ay lastand light, This is a ferly fare to feele. {{right|''York Plays'', p. 58.}}}} {{smaller block|Treuli, treuli, Y seye to ȝou, the sone may not of hym silf do ony thing, but that thing ''that'' he seeth the fadir doynge. {{right|''Wyclif'', John v. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|This holi child seynt Johun, ''That'' baptisid oure lord in flom Jordon With ful deuout & good deuocioun. {{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 56.}}}} {{smaller block|And Guthlake, ''that'' was King of Denmarke then}} [[File:century v08 p0070 c0f1.png|center|355px]] {{c|Tharos Butterfly (''Phyciodes tharos''), natural size.}} to offend.{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 118.}} (''b'') In opposition to ''this'', or by way of distinction. {{smaller block|If the Lord will, we shall live, and do ''this'' or ''that''.{{right|Jas. iv. 15.}}}} {{smaller block|''This'' is not fair; nor profitable ''that''.{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Persius's Satires, iv. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|A hundred and fifty odd projects took possession of his brain by turns—he would do ''this'', and ''that'', and t'other—he would go to Rome—he would go to law—he would buy stock— . . . he would new fore-front his house, and add a new wing to make it even.{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, iv. 31.}}}} {{smaller block|And Guthlake, ''that'' was King of Denmarke then, Provided with a navie mee forlead.{{right|''Mir. for Mags.'', I. 184.}}}} {{smaller block|If I have aught ''That'' may content thee, take it, and begone.{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid's Tragedy, v. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|He ''that'' was your conduct From Milan.{{right|''Shirley'', Grateful Servant, i. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|You shall come with me to Tower Hill, and see Mrs. Quilp ''that'' is, directly.{{right|''Dickens'', Old Curiosity Shop, vi.}}}} In the following extract ''that'', ''who'', and ''which'' are used without any perceptible difference. pearl crescent, ''Phyciodes tharos'', a small Ame varied with black, orange, and '''Thaspium''' (thas′pi-um), ''n.'' ''a'', the carpels.}} '''that''' (ᴛ̵ʜat), ''pron.'' or ''a.''; pl. ''those'' dial. ''thet''; < ME. ''that'', ''thet'', < AS. = OS. ''that'' = OFries. ''thet'', ''dat'' = MLG. ''dat'', that, = OHG. MH = Icel. ''that'', the, = Dan. ''det'', t this, = Goth. ''thata'', the; neut. c pron. which came to be used a AS. masc. ''se'', fem. ''seó'', neut. mod. E. in all genders, ''the'': see ''the''1. Hence ''that'', ''conj.'' and ''adv.'' ''pron.'' or ''a.'' 1. Used as a defin before a noun, in various sense {{smaller|a person or thing present or as before posed to be understood, or used to d thing or person emphatically, having n definite article ''the'', which may, howeve substituted for it.}} {{smaller block|It shall be more tolerable for Sodom the day of judgment than for ''that'' city.}} {{smaller block|Touch but my lips with ''those'' fair {{right|''Shak.'', Venus}}}} {{smaller block|David indeed, by suffering without ''that'' meekness and ''that'' wisdom by adv him much the fitter man to raigne. {{right|''Milton'', E}}}} {{smaller block|''That'' House of Commons that he cou him would do to send him to the Towe {{right|''Wal''}}}} {{smaller block|(''b'') Frequently in opposition to ''this'', in to one of two objects already mentione one more distant in place or time: fr mere contradistinction is implied: a book, and you can take ''that'' one.}} {{smaller block|Of Zion it shall be said, ''this'' and ''tha'' her.}} (c) Pointing not so much to persons an qualities, almost equivalent to ''such'', o and occasionally followed by ''as'' or ''that'' {{smaller block|There cannot be ''That'' vulture in you, to devour {{right|''Shak.'',}}}} When ''this'' and ''that'' refer to foregoing words, ''this'', like the Latin ''hic'' or the French ''ceci'', refers to the last mentioned, the latter, and ''that'', like the Latin ''ille'' or the French ''cela'', to the first mentioned, the former. {{smaller block|Self-love and reason to one end aspire,
Pain their aversion, pleasure their desire;
But greedy ''that'' its object would devour,
''This'' taste the honey and not wound the flower. {{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, ii. 89.}}}} In all the above cases, ''that'', when referring to a plural noun, takes the plural form ''those'': as, ''that'' man, ''those'' men; give me ''that'', give me ''those''; and so on. (''c'') To represent a sentence or part of a sentence, or a series of sentences. {{smaller block|And when Moses heard ''that'', he was content. Lev. x. 20.}} {{smaller block|[''That'' here stands for the whole of what Aaron had said, or the whole of the preceding verse.]}} {{smaller block|I'll know your business, Harry, ''that'' I will. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 3. 83.}} Upon my conscience,
The man is truly honest, and ''that'' kills him. {{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, iv. 3.}} If the Laymen will not come, whose fault is ''that''? {{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 37.}} Certain or uncertain, be ''that'' upon the credit of those whom I must follow. {{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., i.}} They say he's learn'd as well as discreet, but I'm no judge of ''that''. {{right|''Steele'', Lying Lover, i. 1.}} You are a foolish bribble-brabble woman, ''that'' you are. {{right|''Sir R. Howard'', The Committee, iii. 1.}} Yet there still prevails, and ''that'' too amongst men who plume themselves on their liberality, no small amount of the feeling which Milton combated in his celebrated essay. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 167.}}}} ''That'' sometimes in this use precedes the sentence or clause to which it refers. {{smaller block|''That'' be far from thee, to do after this manner, ''to slay the righteous with the wicked.'' {{right|Gen. xviii. 25.}}}} ''That'' here represents the clause in italics. It is used also as the substitute for an adjective: as, you allege that the man is ''innocent''; ''that'' he is not. Similarly, it is often used to introduce an explanation of something going before: as, "religion consists in living up to those principles—''that'' is, in acting in conformity to them." (''d'') Emphatically, in phrases expressive of approbation, applause, or encouragement. {{smaller block|Why, ''that'''s my dainty Ariel! {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, v. 1. 95.}}}} {{smaller block|''That'''s my good son! {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 3. 47.}}}} {{smaller block|''Hengo.'' I have out-brav'd Hunger. ''Car.'' ''That'''s my boy, my sweet boy! {{right|''Fletcher'', Bonduca, iv. 2.}}}} (''e'') As the antecedent of a relative: as, ''that'' which was spoken. {{smaller block|And die, unhallow'd thoughts, before you blot With your uncleanness ''that'' which is divine. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 193.}}}} (''f'') By the omission of the relative, ''that'' formerly sometimes acquired the force of ''what'' or ''that which.'' {{smaller block|Thogh it happen me rehercen eft ''That'' ye han in youre fresshe songes sayd. {{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 79.}}}} {{smaller block|We speak ''that'' we do know, and testify ''that'' we have seen. {{right|John iii. 11.}}}} {{smaller block|The good of my Countrey is ''that'' I seeke. {{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 179.}}}} (''g'') With ''of'', to avoid repetition of a preceding noun: as, his opinions and ''those of'' the others. {{smaller block|I would desire my female readers to consider that, as the term of life is short, ''that of'' beauty is much shorter. {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 89.}}}} (''h'') With ''and'', to avoid repetition of a preceding statement. {{smaller block|God shall help her, ''and that'' right early. {{right|Ps. xlvi. 5.}}}} '''And all that.''' See ''all.''—'''That present.''' See ''present''1.—'''That time†.''' See ''time''1.—'''To put this and that together.''' See ''put''1. '''B.''' ''rel. pron.'' Used for ''who'' or ''which.'' ''That'' in this use is never used with a preposition preceding it, but may be so used when the preposition is transposed to {{smaller block|Sometime like apes, ''that'' mow and chatter at me And after bite me, then like hedgehogs, ''which'' Lie tumbling in my barefoot way and mount Their pricks at my footfall, sometime am I All wound with adders, ''who'' with cloven tongues Do hiss me into madness. ''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 2. 10.}} {{smaller block|With the use of ''that'' as a relative are to be classed those cases in which it is used as a correlative to ''so'' or ''such''.}} {{smaller block|Who 's ''so'' gross, ''That'' seeth not this palpable device? {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 6. 11.}}}} {{smaller block|Who ''so'' firm ''that'' cannot be seduced? {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., i. 2. 316.}}}} {{smaller block|''Such'' allow'd infirmities ''that'' honesty Is never free of. ''Shak.'', W. T., i. 2. 263.}} {{smaller block|''That'' as a demonstrative and ''that'' as a relative pronoun sometimes occur close together, but this use is now hardly approved.}} {{smaller block|''That that'' is determined shall be done. Dan. xi. 36.}} {{smaller block|''That that'' is is. ''Shak.'', T. N., iv. 2. 17.}} {{smaller block|But for the practical part, it is ''that that'' makes an angler: it is diligence, and observation, and patience, and an ambition to be the best in the art, that must do it. {{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 191.}}}} {{smaller block|Frequently used in Chaucer for the definite article, before ''one'' or ''other'', usually when the two words are put in contrast.}} {{smaller block|''That'' on me hette, ''that'' othir dede me colde. {{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 145.}}}} {{smaller block|''That'' . . . ''he''† = who; ''that'' . . . ''his'' (or ''her'')† = whose; ''that'' . . . ''him''† = whom; ''that'' . . . ''they''† = who; ''which that''† = whom.}} {{smaller block|My hertes Ioie, all myn hole plesaunce, ''Whiche that'' y sarue, and schall do faithfully With treue Entente. {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 40.}}}} {{smaller block|A Knight ther was, and that a worthy man, ''That'' fro the tyme that he first bigan To ryden out, ''he'' loved chivalrye. {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 44.}}}} {{smaller block|Now fele I wel the goodnesse of this wyf, ''That'' bothe after her deeth and in her lyf ''Her'' grete bountee doubleth her renoun. {{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 521.}}}} {{smaller block|This man to you may falsly been accused, ''That'' as by right ''him'' oghte been excused. {{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 351.}}}} {{smaller block|[''That'' came in during the twelfth century to supply the place of the indeclinable relative ''the'', and in the fourteenth century it is the ordinary relative. In the sixteenth century, ''which'' often supplies its place; in the seventeenth century, ''who'' replaces it. About Addison's time, ''that'' had again come into fashion, and had almost driven ''which'' and ''who'' out of use. {{right|''Morris'', Historical Outlines of Eng. Accidence, p. 132.]}}}} '''that''' (ᴛ̵ʜat), ''conj.'' [< ME. ''that, thet'', < AS. ''that'' = D. ''dat'' = OHG. MHG. ''daz'', G. ''dass'' = Goth. ''thata'', that; orig. the neut. pron. or adj. ''that'' used practically as a def. article qualifying the whole sentence: see ''that, pron.''] '''1.''' Introducing a reason: in that; because. {{smaller block|Thus I speak, not ''that'' I would have it so; but to your shame. {{right|''Latimer'', Sermon of the Plough.}}}} {{smaller block|Not ''that'' I loved Cæsar less, but ''that'' I loved Rome more. {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iii. 2. 23.}}}} {{smaller block|Streams of grief ''That'' I have wrong'd thee, and as much of joy ''That'' I repent it, issue from mine eyes. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, v. 5.}}}} {{smaller block|It is not ''that'' I love you less Than when before your feet I lay. {{right|''Waller'', The Self-Banished.}}}} {{smaller block|Weep not ''that'' the world changes. {{right|''Bryant'', Mutation.}}}} '''2.''' Introducing an object or final end or purpose: equivalent to the phrases ''in order that'', ''for the purpose that'', ''to the effect that''.
